title: SSF-Net: A Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network for Accurate PDE Operator Learning
authors: Siqi Zhao, Flora D. Salim
abstract: Machine learning methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) significantly improve computational efficiency over traditional numerical solvers such as finite element method (FEM). However, PDE dynamics inherently span both local and global dynamics: disturbances propagate and decay gradually through the domain, while global coupling effects can influence the whole system simultaneously. Capturing both types of dynamics with a low complexity model remains a key challenge. To address this, we propose the Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network (SSF-Net), built around a dual-branch Spatial-Spectral Fusion (SSF) block comprising a spatial branch and a spectral branch. The spatial branch employs a multi-directional Mamba, which mitigates its inherent causal, single-direction scanning bias and capture local interactions with reduced directional bias at linear complexity. The spectral branch leverages a Fourier transform with a block-diagonal MLP to efficiently capture global spectral features with reduced parameter count and complexity. The SSF block is embedded in a multiresolution convolutional encoder-decoder, which extracts multi-scale features. We evaluate SSF-Net on a comprehensive PDE benchmark spanning multiple task types and assess its long-horizon stability. Compared with attention-based and convolution-based baselines, SSF-Net achieves lower prediction error with fewer parameters while retaining near-linear asymptotic complexity in the number of spatial tokens.

infographic.key_insight: SSF-Net combines spatial and spectral processing to learn local interactions and global PDE coupling with near-linear asymptotic complexity in spatial token count.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SSF-Net offers a potential surrogate for repeated FEM-based PDE predictions, though solid-mechanics-specific validation is not established in the abstract.
method: Multi-directional Mamba captures local interactions while reducing directional scanning bias.
Fourier processing with a block-diagonal MLP captures global spectral features efficiently.
A multiresolution convolutional encoder-decoder integrates spatial-spectral fusion blocks across scales.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across a multi-task PDE benchmark with long-horizon stability assessment, SSF-Net reports lower prediction error and fewer parameters than attention- and convolution-based baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy on complex solid-mechanics geometries, boundary conditions, and nonlinear material behavior requires separate validation.
infographic.paper_title: SSF-Net: A Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network for Accurate PDE Operator Learning

title: Mathematical analysis and vectorized FEM implementation of logarithmic strain space framework for finite strains: a case study on elastoplasticity
authors: Miroslav Frost, Martin Kružík, Alexej Moskovka, Jan Valdman
abstract: We investigate the mathematical and computational aspects of the logarithmic strain space framework for finite-strain models in nonlinear continuum mechanics, focusing on the classical von Mises elastoplastic model with linear kinematic hardening. To overcome the lack of coercivity and lower-semicontinuity in the quadratic Hencky energy, we introduce higher-gradient regularization and prove the existence of energetic solutions for rate-independent quasistatic evolution under time-dependent Dirichlet loading. Complementarily, we develop a vectorized MATLAB finite-element implementation of the framework leveraging page-wise matrix functions and operations, and our custom vectorization library. Computational benchmarks show that local tensor operations are significantly accelerated, the logarithmic-strain approach does not substantially increase computational costs, and the implementation robustly handles large rotations and deformations.

infographic.key_insight: Higher-gradient regularization enables an existence proof for finite-strain elastoplastic evolution, while vectorized FEM makes the logarithmic-strain framework computationally practical.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports simulations of elastoplastic solids undergoing large rotations and deformations without substantially increasing computational costs in the reported benchmarks.
method: Use logarithmic strains with von Mises plasticity and linear kinematic hardening.
Introduce higher-gradient regularization and prove existence of energetic solutions under time-dependent Dirichlet loading.
Vectorize MATLAB FEM using page-wise matrix functions and a custom vectorization library.
infographic.evidence_signal: Computational benchmarks report significantly faster local tensor operations and robust handling of large rotations and deformations, but the abstract provides no numerical speedup factors.
infographic.watch_item: The existence result relies on higher-gradient regularization; its parameter choice and discretization require care in practical applications.
infographic.paper_title: Mathematical analysis and vectorized FEM implementation of logarithmic strain space framework for finite strains: a case study on elastoplasticity

title: Finite-strain second-gradient elasticity with an energetic surface: existence of minimizers, incremental theory and elastocapillary beading
authors: Michal Šmejkal, Martin Horák, Martin Kružík
abstract: We develop a finite-strain theory of second-gradient elasticity for solids with a material surface endowed with its own constitutive energy. The bulk second gradient plays two complementary roles. First, under suitable coercivity assumptions and convexity with respect to the second gradient, we prove the existence of minimizers for nonnegative, lower semicontinuous surface energy densities, without requiring convexity, polyconvexity, positive one-homogeneity, or an upper growth bound on the surface energy. Second, it introduces an intrinsic bulk length scale that affects the onset of instability and wavelength selection. To investigate these effects, we derive an incremental small-on-large formulation in the finitely deformed configuration and apply it to the elastocapillary beading of an axially stretched soft cylinder. For an infinite cylinder and the parameters considered, increasing the second-gradient modulus delays bifurcation and shifts the critical mode towards longer wavelengths. Above a finite threshold of this modulus, the critical stretch saturates in the long-wave limit. The model is implemented in the open-source finite element code OOFEM using C1-continuous isogeometric analysis. Finite-cylinder simulations yield onset stretches in close agreement with the analytical predictions. Selected post-bifurcation branches traced by arc-length continuation exhibit beaded states and supercritical bifurcation at small second-gradient moduli, whereas larger moduli are associated with subcritical bifurcation and the formation of distinct thick and thin segments.

infographic.key_insight: Bulk second-gradient elasticity enables minimizer existence under broad surface-energy assumptions while introducing a length scale that delays elastocapillary beading and favors longer wavelengths.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps predict instability onset and beaded morphologies in stretched soft cylinders where surface energy and bulk length-scale effects interact.
method: Prove minimizer existence under suitable bulk coercivity and second-gradient convexity assumptions.
Derive a finite-strain, small-on-large incremental formulation for cylinder stability.
Implement C1-continuous isogeometric analysis in OOFEM and trace post-bifurcation branches by arc-length continuation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Finite-cylinder simulations show onset stretches in close agreement with analytical predictions; selected branches shift from supercritical beading at small second-gradient moduli to subcritical thick–thin segmentation at larger moduli.
infographic.watch_item: Instability trends are reported for the parameters studied, and implementation requires C1-continuous discretizations.
infographic.paper_title: Finite-strain second-gradient elasticity with an energetic surface: existence of minimizers, incremental theory and elastocapillary beading

title: PhyCAD: Physics-Aware Text-to-CAD Generation via Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yuxin Cui, Weijie Zheng, Zhengyang Li, Han Wang, Wenjie Feng, Qiyu Kang
abstract: Language-driven computer-aided design (CAD) generation enables the creation of editable parametric models from text, yet geometric correctness alone does not ensure physical feasibility. We present PhyCAD, a framework for physics-aware Text-to-CAD generation that trains language models to produce executable CadQuery programs under geometric and physical constraints. To support this setting, we construct a Text-to-CAD dataset that links parametric CAD models with geometric specifications, loading conditions, and physical constraints. We further develop an automated CAD--CAE verifier that combines program execution, geometric checks, and finite element analysis to provide feedback for model training. A key learning challenge is to prioritize joint satisfaction of geometric and physical constraints while retaining informative feedback on partial progress. A flat aggregation of heterogeneous rewards can obscure this priority, allowing improvements in individual criteria to compensate for unmet design requirements. We therefore introduce a Hierarchical Balanced Advantage for Group Relative Policy Optimization, grouping candidates into levels according to their verification status and combining between-level progress with objective-wise peer ranking within each level. This formulation preserves cross-level priority in the training signal while providing fine-grained feedback for satisfying constraints and improving feasible designs. Experiments across multiple language models show that PhyCAD consistently improves joint geometric and physical constraint satisfaction. These results demonstrate the value of verifiable engineering feedback for advancing language-driven CAD generation beyond geometric reconstruction toward physics-aware design.

infographic.key_insight: PhyCAD trains text-to-CAD models to prioritize jointly satisfying geometric and physical constraints rather than geometric correctness alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework connects editable CAD generation to finite element verification, helping screen generated designs for specified engineering requirements.
method: Generate executable CadQuery programs from text specifying geometry, loads, and physical constraints.
Verify candidates through program execution, geometric checks, and finite element analysis.
Train with hierarchical GRPO advantages that prioritize verification status while ranking progress within each level.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a dataset linking parametric CAD to engineering specifications and consistent gains in joint constraint satisfaction across multiple language models, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Reliability depends on the CAD–CAE verifier and fidelity of the loading conditions and finite element models.
infographic.paper_title: PhyCAD: Physics-Aware Text-to-CAD Generation via Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning

title: Self-Supervised Learning of Universal Latent Spaces for Operator Learning
authors: Sepehr Mousavi, Levi Lingsch, Siddhartha Mishra, Laura De Lorenzis
abstract: Neural operators fit their representation of functions to the task they are trained on, so every new task rebuilds a reduced space from labeled data. Following the self-supervised pre-training that made representations shareable in natural language processing and computer vision, we decouple representation learning from operator learning. A functional autoencoder is pre-trained on analytic functions synthesized on the fly, with no solver and no labels, to represent functions on arbitrary point clouds, and the latent space it induces is frozen and reused across tasks. The representation is exactly equivariant to translation, dilation, and amplitude, and reconstructs solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) and natural images on geometries it never saw. Being task-agnostic, the latent space can be interpreted in its own right. The whole space is used and decodes to valid fields, it preserves the ordering of distances between physical fields, its geodesics interpolate physical evolutions, and edit directions transfer across fields. With frozen representation maps, a dataset is encoded once and a neural operator is trained entirely on cached embeddings, which saves memory and training time. On 28 tasks in fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, acoustics, and the Helmholtz and Poisson equations, this paradigm can exceed the accuracy of state-of-the-art end-to-end architectures, with up to an order of magnitude higher throughput and memory savings that fit models nearly two orders of magnitude larger on consumer-grade GPUs. At inference, latent rollouts run up to an order of magnitude faster than regular rollouts, and chunked inference processes functions of over half a billion points on a single consumer-grade GPU.

infographic.key_insight: A self-supervised functional autoencoder learns a reusable latent space, separating function representation from task-specific neural operator training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For solid-mechanics surrogates, frozen representations can reduce training memory and accelerate inference without rebuilding the function representation for each task.
method: Pre-train on analytically generated functions without solvers or labels.
Encode arbitrary point clouds with exact translation, dilation, and amplitude equivariance.
Freeze the encoder and decoder, then train task-specific operators on cached embeddings.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 28 tasks spanning solid mechanics, fluids, acoustics, Helmholtz, and Poisson equations, the abstract reports accuracy that can exceed state-of-the-art end-to-end models and up to an order-of-magnitude higher throughput.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer to a specific mechanics application still requires validation of reconstruction fidelity and operator accuracy on its geometries and loading regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Self-Supervised Learning of Universal Latent Spaces for Operator Learning

title: A Tensor-Network Chebyshev-Galerkin Method for Boundary-Value Problems in Computational Mechanics
authors: Juan José Rodríguez-Aldavero, Ángel de la Rosa Velasco, Juan José García-Ripoll
abstract: Quantum-inspired numerical methods for partial differential equations represent discretized fields and operators as quantics tensor trains (QTT), so that their cost depends on how compressible the problem is rather than on the number of unknowns. Global spectral formulations in this setting have so far relied on Fourier bases, restricted to periodic problems, or on collocation, which does not preserve the variational structure exploited by tensor-network solvers. We introduce a QTT Chebyshev-Galerkin method that assembles and solves global spectral systems directly in compressed form, without forming the underlying arrays. Starting from the weak formulation, the method handles coupled elliptic systems with variable coefficients, smoothly mapped geometries, and mixed Dirichlet-Robin boundary conditions, and yields symmetric positive-definite systems suited to variational tensor-network solvers. Parameters and random inputs enter as additional coordinates, so the same construction returns the solution over an entire parameter space in a single solve. In linear elasticity, the method retains spectral convergence and reaches errors below $10^{-8}$ on a three-dimensional benchmark, beyond those attained by QTT finite differences and Q2/Q4 FEniCSx finite elements over the tested range. A six-parameter cantilever design study covering $1.7\times10^{7}$ designs is solved in a single 92s run, and a stochastic problem with ten random coordinates is represented with $2.4\times10^{6}$ times less memory than its full coefficient array.

infographic.key_insight: A quantics tensor-train (QTT) Chebyshev–Galerkin method solves global spectral boundary-value problems directly in compressed form while preserving their variational structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables accurate elasticity analysis across large design and uncertainty spaces without explicitly storing every field coefficient.
method: Assemble weak-form spectral systems directly in QTT format without forming full arrays.
Handle coupled elliptic systems, variable coefficients, smooth geometry mappings, and mixed Dirichlet–Robin boundaries.
Treat parameters and random inputs as additional coordinates to solve entire parameter spaces at once.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported results include errors below 10⁻⁸ on a 3D elasticity benchmark, 1.7×10⁷ cantilever designs solved in 92 seconds, and 2.4×10⁶-fold memory reduction for a problem with ten random coordinates.
infographic.watch_item: Efficiency depends on tensor compressibility; the reported benchmarks do not establish comparable gains for poorly compressible problems.
infographic.paper_title: A Tensor-Network Chebyshev-Galerkin Method for Boundary-Value Problems in Computational Mechanics

title: Finite Element Elastographic Analysis of Kidney MRI for Computational Assessment of Chronic Kidney Disease
authors: A. Bhattacharjee, M. M. Rahman, A. Srivastava, E. H. Bhuiyan
abstract: Background and Objective: Bridging kidney MRI with patient-specific computational biomechanics may enable accurate, noninvasive assessment of chronic kidney disease. To develop a finite element method (FEM)-based computational elastography framework for estimating renal biomechanical properties from conventional kidney MRI and to evaluate its ability to differentiate chronic kidney disease (CKD) from healthy controls. Methods: Kidney segmentation masks from healthy control and CKD subjects were converted into triangulated surface meshes, and watertight surfaces were tetrahedralized to create volumetric FEM meshes. Kidney tissue was modeled as a nearly incompressible Kelvin-Voigt viscoelastic material. Harmonic wave propagation simulations were performed using FEM, followed by Helmholtz-based elastographic inversion to estimate complex shear modulus distributions. Derived biomechanical parameters were used for CKD classification using machine learning models. Results: FEM-derived stiffness estimates showed consistency with stiffness ranges previously reported in human renal MRE studies and also showed measurable differences between healthy and CKD groups. Machine learning models trained on FEM-derived features achieved classification performance up to 86.26% cross-validation accuracy with an AUC of 0.92. Conclusion: FEM-derived elastographic parameters showed potential for distinguishing CKD from healthy tissue and may provide an alternative for renal biomechanical assessment without dedicated MRE acquisition.

infographic.key_insight: MRI-derived kidney FEM models produced elastographic features that distinguished CKD from healthy controls with up to 86.26% cross-validation accuracy and an AUC of 0.92.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework links conventional kidney MRI to computational biomechanics without requiring dedicated magnetic resonance elastography acquisition.
method: Convert kidney segmentation masks into watertight surfaces and tetrahedral FEM meshes.
Simulate harmonic waves using a nearly incompressible Kelvin–Voigt viscoelastic tissue model.
Estimate complex shear modulus via Helmholtz inversion and classify CKD using derived biomechanical features.
infographic.evidence_signal: Healthy and CKD subjects showed measurable differences in FEM-derived stiffness, with estimates consistent with previously reported human renal MRE ranges.
infographic.watch_item: Agreement with published stiffness ranges is not patient-specific mechanical validation; estimates may depend on assumed material properties and simulation conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Finite Element Elastographic Analysis of Kidney MRI for Computational Assessment of Chronic Kidney Disease

title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion
authors: Li Zheng, Simin Chen
abstract: Finite element method (FEM) solvers are foundational to scientific and engineering simulation, yet their susceptibility to \emph{efficiency attacks} remains largely unexplored. An adversary can craft syntactically valid and runnable FEM programs that complete successfully while forcing excessive computational work, enabling computational denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Finding such inputs is challenging because FEM programs occupy a vast, structured space constrained by numerical, geometric, and constitutive requirements. We introduce CloakFEM, a domain-guided LLM-agent framework for automatically generating runnable adversarial FEM programs that amplify solver computation. CloakFEM combines LLM-guided search with an FEM-specific intermediate representation and a deterministic validity gate that enforces runnable constraints. Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM discovers adversarial inputs that substantially amplify solver work while remaining valid and solvable. In the most extreme case, solver iterations increase from 43 to 247,367, a \(5{,}752.72\times\) amplification. CloakFEM outperforms five generic black-box baselines and retains an advantage over evolutionary search under a controlled bounded action space. Cross-solver analysis further reveals both problem-intrinsic and solver-specific sources of vulnerability. Our results uncover an underexplored efficiency-attack surface in FEM solvers and show that runnable FEM programs can serve as adversarial inputs.

infographic.key_insight: CloakFEM shows that valid, solvable FEM programs can act as efficiency attacks, increasing solver iterations by up to 5,752.72×.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Simulation services may face computational denial-of-service risks from FEM inputs that run successfully but consume excessive solver resources.
method: Use a domain-guided LLM agent to search for computationally expensive FEM programs.
Represent candidates with an FEM-specific intermediate representation.
Apply a deterministic validity gate to enforce runnable constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM outperformed five generic black-box baselines; the most extreme case increased solver iterations from 43 to 247,367.
infographic.watch_item: Iteration amplification is not necessarily proportional to wall-clock slowdown, and vulnerability can depend on the solver and problem.
infographic.paper_title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion

title: SparseModesNet for coupled thermal-hydraulic-mechanical system in heterogeneous porous media
authors: Kapil Chawla, Tomoki Koike, Sanghyun Lee, Julie Bessac
abstract: Coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) models describe interactions among displacement, fluid pressure, and temperature in geothermal systems. Fine-mesh simulations over many time steps are costly, particularly with heterogeneous permeability and thermal conductivity or fracture networks that alter fluid and heat transport. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) reduces the number of unknowns but can require many modes because its reconstruction is linear. We apply SparseModesNet to reconstruct coupled THM solutions using a small set of selected modes and a neural-network nonlinear decoder. Starting from a larger collection of candidate modes, SparseModesNet selects modes to reduce reconstruction error rather than simply retaining those with the highest energy. We compare SparseModesNet with POD on three problems: a two-dimensional heterogeneous medium, a two-dimensional connected fracture network, and a three-dimensional geometry based on Utah FORGE fractures. We evaluate reconstructed displacement, pressure, and temperature fields, as well as pressure- and temperature-based quantities of interest. We also test temporal interpolation by training on a subset of snapshots and reconstructing omitted snapshots within the same time interval. For the same reduced dimension, SparseModesNet achieves smaller reconstruction errors than POD and accurately recovers the solution fields and selected geothermal quantities of interest.

infographic.key_insight: SparseModesNet reconstructs coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical fields more accurately than linear POD at the same reduced dimension by selecting modes for reconstruction quality and using a nonlinear neural decoder.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact representations of displacement, pressure, and temperature could support efficient analysis of heterogeneous and fractured geothermal systems.
method: Start with a larger pool of candidate modes.
Select a small mode set to reduce reconstruction error rather than retain only the highest-energy modes.
Use a neural-network nonlinear decoder to reconstruct coupled solution fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covers a 2D heterogeneous medium, a 2D connected fracture network, and a 3D Utah FORGE-based geometry, including field errors, geothermal quantities of interest, and temporal interpolation of omitted snapshots.
infographic.watch_item: Temporal testing addresses interpolation within the training time interval; extrapolation and generalization to unseen geological configurations are not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: SparseModesNet for coupled thermal-hydraulic-mechanical system in heterogeneous porous media

title: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Coarse-to-Fine Finite Element Solver for Heterogeneous Darcy Flow
authors: Kapil Chawla, Sanghyun Lee, Jonathan Valyou
abstract: Quantum linear system algorithms offer theoretical potential for solving large sparse systems from PDE discretizations. However, applying them directly to fine-scale problems remains impractical on near-term hardware because of limited qubits, restricted circuit depth, and noise. They also prepare a quantum state rather than solution coefficients, whose recovery requires measurement and reconstruction. In this work, we develop a hybrid quantum-classical coarse-to-fine finite element framework for heterogeneous Darcy flow. We investigate whether a measured quantum coarse solution improves fine-grid initialization and reduces subsequent classical solver work. Rather than solve the full fine-scale system on a quantum device, we apply a method inspired by the Variational Quantum Linear Solver (VQLS) to the Galerkin coarse system. We reconstruct the approximate coarse solution from measurements, prolongate it to the fine grid, and use it to initialize a classical preconditioned iterative solve.} Numerical experiments on steady heterogeneous Darcy flow and a time-dependent SPE10-based problem show that measured quantum coarse solutions can improve fine-grid initialization, while classical correction recovers accurate pressure fields. The effect on classical solver iterations depends on the problem. All quantum computations were simulated using Qiskit Aer.

infographic.key_insight: A measured quantum coarse-grid solution can improve fine-grid initialization for heterogeneous Darcy flow, with classical correction recovering accurate pressure fields.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework explores quantum-assisted finite element solvers for heterogeneous porous-media flow without placing the full fine-scale system on quantum hardware.
method: Apply a VQLS-inspired method to the Galerkin coarse system.
Reconstruct coarse solution coefficients from quantum measurements and prolongate them to the fine grid.
Initialize a classical preconditioned iterative solver with the prolonged solution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on steady heterogeneous Darcy flow and a time-dependent SPE10-based problem showed improved initialization, but iteration reductions depended on the problem; all quantum computations used Qiskit Aer simulation.
infographic.watch_item: Hardware performance and net computational advantage remain unestablished, particularly when measurement and reconstruction costs are included.
infographic.paper_title: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Coarse-to-Fine Finite Element Solver for Heterogeneous Darcy Flow

title: Geometric Multigrid Preconditioners for conforming Finite Element Methods on Arbitrarily Agglomerated Meshes
authors: Santiago Badia, Jordi Manyer
abstract: Geometric multigrid methods for conforming finite element discretisations classically require a nested mesh hierarchy, forcing coarse meshes to be conforming, which is unsuitable for general domains. In order to eliminate this geometric constraint, we introduce and analyse a family of multilevel auxiliary space preconditioners. At the first level, a conforming Lagrangian discretisation on a fine simplicial mesh is preconditioned by a non-conforming polytopal discretisation posed on an arbitrarily agglomerated coarse mesh. At the subsequent levels, the coarse problem is solved by a geometric multigrid method for that polytopal discretisation on further agglomerated meshes, so that the whole hierarchy is generated from the fine mesh by agglomeration alone. We consider two polytopal discretisations, a symmetric interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method and a hybrid high-order method. The prolongation operator at the first level is an element-wise interpolation onto the fine mesh followed by nodal averaging, preceded in the hybrid high-order case by a local potential reconstruction. For point-Jacobi and vertex-star patch additive Schwarz smoothers, we prove that the condition number of the preconditioned system is bounded by $O((H/h)^3)$, where $H/h$ is the coarsening ratio, and by $O((H/h)^2)$ for the DG variant with penalty proportional to $H/h$. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions, on structured and unstructured meshes with agglomerates generated by automatic clustering algorithms, confirm the robustness of the preconditioners.

infographic.key_insight: Auxiliary-space multigrid preconditioners remove the need for nested conforming coarse meshes by building the hierarchy through arbitrary mesh agglomeration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports efficient iterative solution of conforming finite element systems on complex domains without constructing conforming coarse meshes.
method: Precondition fine-mesh conforming Lagrangian FEM with a coarse polytopal DG or hybrid high-order discretisation.
Build subsequent multigrid levels by further agglomeration.
Transfer coarse solutions using element-wise interpolation and nodal averaging, with local potential reconstruction for the hybrid high-order variant.
infographic.evidence_signal: Two- and three-dimensional experiments on structured and unstructured meshes with automatically clustered agglomerates confirm robustness; proven condition-number bounds scale as O((H/h)^3), improving to O((H/h)^2) for DG with appropriately scaled penalty.
infographic.watch_item: The condition-number bounds worsen with the coarsening ratio H/h, so aggressive agglomeration can affect solver performance.
infographic.paper_title: Geometric Multigrid Preconditioners for conforming Finite Element Methods on Arbitrarily Agglomerated Meshes

title: Mass-lumped finite elements with maximum-bound preservation and original-energy dissipation for the degenerate-mobility Allen-Cahn equation
authors: Himanshu Kumar Dwivedi, Matthias Ehrhardt
abstract: In this work, we propose a mass-lumped finite element method for the Allen-Cahn equation that incorporates nonlinear mobility which may degenerate. The spatial approximation uses continuous, piecewise linear, mass-lumped finite elements, while convex splitting is employed for the double-well potential in time. Under the standard non-obtuse mesh condition, it is shown that the resulting fully discrete method preserves the maximum-bound principle unconditionally: if the initial approximation takes values in $[-1, 1]$, then so does the numerical solution at every time level. Additionally, the method dissipates the original discrete Ginzburg-Landau energy without any time-step restriction, even when the mobility vanishes at pure phases. This analysis relies on the monotonicity of the lumped finite element operator and the convexity of the split potential. Numerical experiments confirm these theoretical properties and demonstrate the robustness of the method in phase-separation dynamics involving degenerate mobility.

infographic.key_insight: A mass-lumped finite element scheme preserves phase-field values in [-1, 1] and dissipates the original discrete energy without time-step restrictions, even with degenerate mobility.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports robust phase-separation simulations by maintaining physical bounds and energy decay when mobility vanishes at pure phases.
method: Use continuous, piecewise-linear, mass-lumped finite elements on non-obtuse meshes.
Apply convex splitting to the double-well potential in time.
Establish bound preservation and energy dissipation using operator monotonicity and split-potential convexity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments confirming the theoretical properties and robustness in degenerate-mobility phase-separation dynamics, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees rely on a non-obtuse mesh condition; unconditional stability does not imply time-step-independent accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Mass-lumped finite elements with maximum-bound preservation and original-energy dissipation for the degenerate-mobility Allen-Cahn equation

title: Locating Contact on Tendon-Driven Continuum Robots From Tendon Measurements Alone via Constrained Moving Horizon Estimation
authors: Haitham El-Hussieny
abstract: Tendon-driven continuum robots can reach through constrained spaces, but contact along their bodies is invisible to the sensors at their motors. We show that this is a structural limitation rather than a tuning problem: the map from contact forces to tendon measurements has a null space of dimension at least seven, so no estimator that leaves the contact support free can locate contact. When the obstacle geometry is known, however, non-penetration and complementarity make the contact force locally identifiable, and we prove that the resulting system with unknown contact inputs is locally exponentially strongly detectable. We present a constrained moving horizon estimator (MHE) that encodes these conditions and runs in real time as one quadratic program per sample, and we give a local, mode-wise robust stability result for it. In a finite- element benchmark of a two-section robot pressing and sliding on a wall, the estimator located contact to 0.9 mm and estimated contact force to 0.22 N, compared with 65 mm and 0.72 N for a tuned extended Kalman filter (EKF) with state projection. The estimator tolerated millimeter- level errors in the obstacle position and unmodeled wall friction, under which the projected EKF failed. Under randomized model mismatch over 40 trials, including unmodeled tendon friction, it remained better in force and location in every trial. Without contact, the MHE offered no advantage over the EKF, which confirms that its benefit comes from the contact constraints. This report extends a letter submitted to IEEE Control Systems Letters with complete proofs and additional experiments.

infographic.key_insight: Tendon measurements alone cannot locate unrestricted contact, but known obstacle geometry and contact constraints can make contact forces locally identifiable.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Geometry-aware estimation could enable tendon-driven continuum robots to infer body contact without adding distributed contact sensors.
method: Prove a contact-to-measurement null space of dimension at least seven.
Enforce non-penetration and complementarity in constrained moving horizon estimation.
Solve one quadratic program per sample, with local detectability and mode-wise robust stability guarantees.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a finite-element wall-contact benchmark, MHE achieved 0.9 mm location error and 0.22 N force error versus 65 mm and 0.72 N for a projected EKF, and outperformed it on both metrics in all 40 randomized model-mismatch trials.
infographic.watch_item: The approach relies on known obstacle geometry; guarantees are local and mode-wise, and the reported evaluation is simulation-based.
infographic.paper_title: Locating Contact on Tendon-Driven Continuum Robots From Tendon Measurements Alone via Constrained Moving Horizon Estimation

title: Finite-element reconstruction of molten-zone dynamics and chemical segregation in optical floating-zone grown Ni--Mn--Ga
authors: Denys Musiienko, Taras Kovaliuk, Petr Harcuba, Oleg Heczko, Ross H. Colman
abstract: Homogeneous single-crystal growth of Ni--Mn--Ga magnetic shape-memory alloys is limited by incongruent melting, Mn reactivity, and longitudinal composition segregation. We report a modified optical floating-zone method in which growth is performed inside a transparent sapphire crucible, stabilising the molten zone while preserving optical heating and visual monitoring. The resulting crystals show improved growth reproducibility and controlled macroscopic geometry. To interpret the measured segregation profiles, a transient finite-element heat-transfer model in COMSOL Multiphysics was coupled to an effective molten-zone mass-balance calculation. The model reveals that the local solidification velocity is not fixed by the imposed translation speed but varies strongly as the molten-zone geometry evolves. The calculated solidification-front geometry is independently supported by EBSD analysis of a quenched growth interface, while the coupled mass-balance calculation reproduces the dominant features of the measured composition profiles. These results show that deviations from ideal Scheil--Pfann behaviour arise from the evolving molten-zone geometry and solidification conditions. The experimentally constrained model therefore provides a practical means of reconstructing otherwise inaccessible growth conditions and a basis for optimisation of sapphire-confined floating-zone growth of incongruently melting alloys.

infographic.key_insight: Evolving molten-zone geometry changes local solidification velocity, helping explain chemical segregation in Ni–Mn–Ga beyond ideal Scheil–Pfann behaviour.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Sapphire-confined optical floating-zone growth improves reproducibility and macroscopic geometry control, while modelling supports optimisation toward more homogeneous crystals.
method: Stabilise the optically heated molten zone inside a transparent sapphire crucible.
Couple transient COMSOL finite-element heat transfer to an effective molten-zone mass balance.
Reconstruct solidification-front evolution and longitudinal composition profiles.
infographic.evidence_signal: EBSD of a quenched interface independently supports the calculated front geometry, and the coupled model reproduces dominant features of measured composition profiles.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no quantitative prediction errors, so reconstruction accuracy and transferability to other growth conditions remain unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Finite-element reconstruction of molten-zone dynamics and chemical segregation in optical floating-zone grown Ni--Mn--Ga

title: Optimal stability estimates and preasymptotic error analysis of the CIP-FEM for the Helmholtz equation with uniaxial perfectly matched layers
authors: Silin Wen, Yu Du
abstract: We study the uniaxial perfectly matched layer (UPML) problem for the Helmholtz equation in two and three dimensions and establish wavenumber-explicit stability estimates at high wavenumbers. For the full-space UPML problem, we prove the optimal stability estimate with the inf-sup constant satisfying $μ_\infty\eqsim k^{-1}$ for sufficiently large $k$ if the absorption function $σ\in W^{1,\infty}$ is a piecewise-power function of order at least one for which $\|σ'\|_{L^\infty(\{t:0<σ(t)\leqδ_*\})}\leq \varepsilon_*$, where $\varepsilon_*$ and $δ_*$ depend only on the PML parameters. Using this stability estimate, we obtain the optimal inf-sup estimate $μ_L\eqsim k^{-1}$ for the truncated UPML problem. These estimates further yield preasymptotic error estimates for a linear continuous interior penalty finite element method (CIP-FEM). Numerical simulations confirmed the theoretical predictions and demonstrated the effectiveness of CIP-FEM under high-wavenumber conditions.

infographic.key_insight: For high-wavenumber Helmholtz problems in 2D and 3D, the paper proves optimal inf-sup scaling μ ≍ k⁻¹ for both full-space and truncated uniaxial perfectly matched layers under specified absorption-profile conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results support reliable finite element simulation of high-frequency wave propagation using absorbing layers to truncate unbounded domains.
method: Establish wavenumber-explicit stability for full-space UPML with admissible piecewise-power absorption profiles.
Transfer the optimal inf-sup estimate to truncated UPML domains.
Derive preasymptotic error estimates for linear continuous interior penalty FEM.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations confirm the theoretical predictions and demonstrate CIP-FEM effectiveness at high wavenumbers, though the abstract gives no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The stability guarantees require specific absorption-profile regularity and derivative bounds near the onset of absorption; they do not cover arbitrary UPML profiles.
infographic.paper_title: Optimal stability estimates and preasymptotic error analysis of the CIP-FEM for the Helmholtz equation with uniaxial perfectly matched layers

title: Process-zone condensation: a discretization-exact reduced cell model for FE$^2$ analysis of composites with fibre-matrix debonding and matrix plasticity
authors: Leonilson Toffoli Pedrini, Maycoln Conci, Rafael Marin Ferro
abstract: Periodic composites with cohesive interfaces and matrix plasticity require nonlinear cell solutions in multiscale analysis. Process-zone condensation eliminates the linear elastic remainder of the cell by a Schur complement, retaining all interfacial and process-zone internal variables. Influence matrices recover macroscopic stress and consistent tangent. One back-substitution per increment checks that the matrix outside the retained zone remains elastic. While this holds, the reduction is exact relative to the full discretisation, also with a plastic matrix, and requires no training. In an E-glass/epoxy cell, eight of nine two-dimensional paths agree with the full cell to 1e-11 in stress and tangent; the check flags the ninth. Three paths on each of two three-dimensional meshes need zone expansion. Excluding setup and checks, two-dimensional path timings show an aggregate speed-up of 3.3; certified three-dimensional zones show none. In adaptive finite element squared (FE$^2$) simulations of a perforated plate, the reduced solver reproduces the full-cell response within solver tolerances, 1.51 times faster for glass/polypropylene and slower for glass/epoxy. Independent Ansys models agree to below 1e-3 in cell stress and about 0.6% in plate reactions, although local damage and plasticity onsets differ. The advantage depends on zone size, active set and adaptation costs.

infographic.key_insight: Process-zone condensation exactly reproduces the full discretized composite cell while plasticity stays inside the retained zone, without training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method can accelerate FE² simulations of composites with fibre–matrix debonding and matrix plasticity while preserving macroscopic stress and consistent tangent.
method: Eliminate the linear elastic cell remainder using a Schur complement.
Retain interface and process-zone variables; recover stress and tangent through influence matrices.
Back-substitute once per increment to check that the eliminated matrix remains elastic.
infographic.evidence_signal: Eight of nine 2D paths matched full-cell stress and tangent to 1e-11; aggregate 2D speed-up was 3.3× excluding setup and checks, while plate simulations were 1.51× faster for glass/polypropylene but slower for glass/epoxy.
infographic.watch_item: Exactness requires the eliminated region to remain elastic; zone expansion and adaptation costs can erase speed gains, as seen in the certified 3D cases.
infographic.paper_title: Process-zone condensation: a discretization-exact reduced cell model for FE$^2$ analysis of composites with fibre-matrix debonding and matrix plasticity

title: AlterNet: Adaptive-Depth Mixture-of-Experts with Learned Halting for Elastic Inference
authors: Alexander Kastius
abstract: Most LLM architectures have fixed compute demands determined at training time. We propose a novel architecture that combines the Mixture-of-Experts architecture with shallow experts and a novel dynamic-depth system to make the extent of a forward pass dynamically adjustable. Our approach lets the model automatically determine the compute needed for a given task, paired with a system to scale it down after training without retraining when the execution environment demands faster or cheaper inference. To achieve this, we introduce an iterative computation mechanism, sequence-level depth-based routing steered by a halting mechanism within the experts, a depth encoding that lets the model track its progress in the chain, and a regularization mechanism that incentivizes the model to use allocated compute efficiently. We present initial benchmarks and discuss future research directions.

infographic.key_insight: AlterNet combines shallow mixture-of-experts modules with learned halting to adapt inference depth and reduce compute after training without retraining.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive inference could help fit engineering AI workloads to latency and compute budgets, although the abstract reports no solid-mechanics-specific validation.
method: Iterative computation with sequence-level, depth-based expert routing.
Learned halting within experts and depth encoding to track progress.
Regularization to encourage efficient use of allocated compute.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract mentions initial benchmarks but provides no datasets, quantitative results, or accuracy–compute trade-offs.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy under reduced compute and practical latency gains remain unclear from the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: AlterNet: Adaptive-Depth Mixture-of-Experts with Learned Halting for Elastic Inference

title: Remap for ALE Hydrodynamics via Direct Interpolation and Constraint Optimization
authors: Brendan Keith, Dohyun Kim, Boyan Lazarov, Ketan Mittal, Cosmin G. Petra, Mathias R. Schmidt
abstract: This work presents an optimization-based remap approach for arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) hydrodynamics that preserves sharp features and physical bounds while conserving global quantities such as volume, mass, momentum, and total energy. Achieving these properties is the main challenge in remap methods. The presented approach is well-suited for high-order finite element (FE) discretizations and ALE methods that allow for large, purely Lagrangian displacements between successive remeshing and remapping steps. Recent advances in parallel, GPU-capable interpolation routines enable the initial transfer of all fields via direct physical-space interpolation, avoiding computationally costly and diffusive pseudo-transient PDE-based advection. The interpolation produces bounded fields with minimal numerical diffusion. However, it may violate the desired conservation of global properties. Thus, a subsequent optimization step restores conservation while preserving physical bounds. The presented method provides minimally diffusive remapping of finite element fields of arbitrary order. Moreover, it directly remaps quantities defined at integration points, eliminating the need for projection onto finite element spaces. The approach also mitigates typical challenges associated with synchronizing primal variables and conserved quantities in advection-based remap methods. The proposed optimization-based remap method is evaluated using standard two- and three-dimensional remap benchmarks and full ALE hydrodynamics simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Direct interpolation followed by constraint optimization enables minimally diffusive ALE remapping while enforcing physical bounds and global conservation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports high-order hydrodynamics simulations with large Lagrangian mesh displacements while preserving sharp features and conserving volume, mass, momentum, and total energy.
method: Transfer fields through direct physical-space interpolation rather than pseudo-transient PDE advection.
Restore global conservation through optimization while preserving physical bounds.
Remap arbitrary-order finite element fields and integration-point quantities without intermediate projection.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation on standard 2D and 3D remap benchmarks and full ALE hydrodynamics simulations, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify the conservation-correction optimization's computational cost or parallel scalability.
infographic.paper_title: Remap for ALE Hydrodynamics via Direct Interpolation and Constraint Optimization

title: Trapping and Fracture of Particles in Three-Sphere Ball-Milling Collisions
authors: Ziyi Cui, Qiong Zhang, Suwei Liu, Richard M. Lueptow
abstract: We numerically investigate the collision and fracture processes of ball milling based on a minimal model of a three-sphere geometry using discrete element method (DEM) simulations combined with Christensen-type and Weibull-type normalized fracture criteria. The outcome of the brittle target particle (ejected versus trapped, fractured versus intact) depends on the impact geometry and velocity. We develop a reduced three-sphere collision description in which trapping is governed by impact geometry and friction, while fracture inside the trapping regime is evaluated from DEM output using stress-based and contact-force-based normalized criteria. The trapping regime follows a closed-form geometric condition, while the critical conditions for fracture vary with impact angle, obliquity angle, impact velocity, and particle size ratio. Head-on collisions with larger size ratios require lower critical impact velocities for fracture.

infographic.key_insight: A minimal three-sphere model separates geometry- and friction-controlled particle trapping from fracture, with head-on collisions at larger size ratios requiring lower critical impact velocities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model can inform ball-milling impact conditions that favor particle capture and breakage rather than ejection.
method: Simulate three-sphere collisions using the discrete element method (DEM).
Describe trapping with a closed-form geometric condition accounting for friction.
Evaluate fracture from DEM output using Christensen-type stress and Weibull-type contact-force normalized criteria.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations link trapping and fracture outcomes to impact geometry and velocity, with fracture thresholds varying with impact angle, obliquity, and particle size ratio.
infographic.watch_item: The minimal three-sphere geometry may not capture collective interactions in a full mill, and the abstract reports no experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Trapping and Fracture of Particles in Three-Sphere Ball-Milling Collisions

title: A Second-Order Semi-Implicit Projection Time-Stepping Scheme for the Shallow-Water Equations on the Sphere Using Compatible Finite Elements
authors: Karina Kowalczyk, Colin Cotter
abstract: We propose a second-order, semi-implicit time-stepping scheme for the shallow-water equations on the sphere discretised with compatible finite elements. The scheme splits the advection operator from the wave operator, applying a DG-upwind SSPRK3 method to the advection part and an $H(\text{div})$-conforming implicit discretisation to the wave part, solved efficiently via hybridisation. The scheme follows a three-step symmetric splitting: an explicit half-step, a full advection step, and an implicit half-step that simultaneously projects the velocity back into the $H(\text{div})$ space. This symmetry guarantees global second-order accuracy and confines the stability restriction to the CFL condition of the advection step alone. The time-step can therefore be extended beyond this limit by subcycling the advection step without additional implicit solves. The method is implemented in Firedrake and validated against a standard suite of spherical shallow-water benchmarks, demonstrating stable results for Courant numbers up to 1 (with two advection subcycles) with second-order finite elements, second-order convergence, and good parallel scaling.

infographic.key_insight: A symmetric semi-implicit projection scheme achieves second-order time accuracy for spherical shallow-water equations while restricting stability by advection rather than fast waves.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports larger time steps for geophysical flow simulations by subcycling advection without adding implicit wave solves.
method: Use compatible finite elements with DG-upwind SSPRK3 advection.
Apply an explicit half-step, full advection step, and implicit half-step that projects velocity into H(div).
Solve the implicit wave system efficiently through hybridisation in Firedrake.
infographic.evidence_signal: Standard spherical shallow-water benchmarks demonstrate second-order convergence, good parallel scaling, and stable results at Courant numbers up to 1 with two advection subcycles and second-order finite elements.
infographic.watch_item: Advection remains CFL-limited; larger overall time steps require subcycling, which adds explicit computational work.
infographic.paper_title: A Second-Order Semi-Implicit Projection Time-Stepping Scheme for the Shallow-Water Equations on the Sphere Using Compatible Finite Elements
